summary: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs).

eli5.summary: Tiny wireless sensors need a standard way to be checked and adjusted from afar. This RFC defines the labeled settings and readings for such sensor networks.

subtitle: A MIB module of read-only counters that shows how a node's 6LoWPAN layer receives, compresses, fragments and forwards datagrams.

tldr.problem: There were MIB modules for UDP, IP and interfaces, but nothing for monitoring and troubleshooting the 6LoWPAN layer that sits between IPv6 and low-power radio links.
tldr.mechanism: The LOWPAN-MIB module, registered as lowpanMIB { mib-2 226 }, defines 29 read-only Counter32-style statistics (the first is a timeout) twice: once globally and once per interface.
tldr.outcome: Operators can see how many datagrams were received, reassembled, decompressed, fragmented, mesh-forwarded or discarded. The module has no writable objects.

today: RFC 7388 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2014, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Management Framework
sections.content:
This RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs, RFC 4944). A MIB module gives direct access to data through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), but the RFC notes that SNMP may not always be affordable on constrained devices. Other protocols can also access data modeled in MIB modules, and bindings to the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) have been proposed.

The module follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework and is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).
sections.eli5: Network gadgets need a standard way to be asked how they are doing. This RFC writes down the questions you can ask a tiny wireless network about one of its jobs.

sections.title: Where the Module Fits
sections.content:
The RFC lines up the IETF protocols for constrained devices (CoAP, UDP, IPv6 with ICMPv6, 6LoWPAN, and IEEE 802.15.4 and similar links) next to the MIB modules that monitor them: UDP-MIB, IP-MIB, IP-FORWARD-MIB and IF-MIB. LOWPAN-MIB fills the hole at the 6LoWPAN layer.

The module is primarily a collection of counters that reflect how 6LoWPAN datagrams are processed. For link layers that use the dispatch byte from RFC 4944, a 6LoWPAN datagram is one whose dispatch byte matches 01xxxxxx, 10xxxxxx or 11xxxxxx. Datagrams matching 00xxxxxx (NALP, not a LoWPAN frame) are not counted as 6LoWPAN datagrams. Other radio technologies may identify 6LoWPAN datagrams differently.
sections.eli5: The wireless layer is one floor in a building of network layers. This module puts a counter on that floor so you can tell what is happening there.

sections.title: Object Tree and Statistics Tables
sections.content:
The module sits at lowpanMIB { mib-2 226 } and has three parts: lowpanNotifications, lowpanObjects and lowpanConformance. Under lowpanObjects, lowpanStats holds the global statistics as seen by the 6LoWPAN layer. lowpanIfStatsTable holds the same set of objects per interface, indexed by ifIndex. Each set has 29 objects. The per-interface statistics are optional to implement.

The first object, lowpanReasmTimeout, is an Unsigned32 in seconds: the maximum time received fragments are held awaiting reassembly. The other 28 are read-only Counter32 values.
sections.eli5: There is one big scoreboard for the whole device, and optionally one smaller scoreboard for each network connection it has.

sections.title: What the Counters Measure
sections.content:
The counters follow a datagram through the layer. Incoming counters cover receipt (InReceives, InHdrErrors), mesh handling (InMeshReceives, InMeshForwds, InMeshDelivers), reassembly (InReasmReqds, InReasmFails, InReasmOKs), header decompression (InCompReqds, InCompFails, InCompOKs) and delivery to IPv6 (InDelivers). Outgoing counters mirror them for requests, compression, fragmentation (OutFragReqds, OutFragFails, OutFragOKs, OutFragCreates), mesh routing problems (OutMeshHopLimitExceeds, OutMeshNoRoutes) and transmission.

The fragmentation counters are modeled after those of the IP-MIB (RFC 4293). The generic InDiscards and OutDiscards counters can be incremented any time a datagram is dropped for a reason that no more specific counter covers, for example when all buffers are in use for ongoing reassemblies.

The processing diagram is conceptual. For incoming datagrams compression happens after reassembly, and for outgoing ones before fragmentation, but implementations may differ, for example by decompressing FRAG1 fragments as soon as they arrive. Implementations that do not support mesh forwarding MUST count received datagrams with a MESH header in lowpanInMeshReceives, but MUST NOT increment lowpanInMeshReceives and lowpanInMeshDelivers if those datagrams are dropped.
sections.eli5: Each counter is a tally mark for one step: packet arrived, glued back together, unpacked, handed on, or thrown away. Comparing tallies shows where packets get lost.

sections.title: Conformance Groups
sections.content:
The module defines four object groups and one compliance statement. lowpanStatsGroup and lowpanIfStatsGroup cover the counters without mesh handling. lowpanStatsMeshGroup and lowpanIfStatsMeshGroup cover the counters for datagrams with a MESH header.

In the compliance statement, the per-interface group is mandatory for implementations that expose per-interface statistics. The per-interface mesh group is mandatory for those that also process or forward datagrams with a MESH header.
sections.eli5: The groups are checklists. A device only needs to keep the tallies for the features it actually has.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in the module has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, so if the module is implemented correctly an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through SNMP SET operations. Readable objects may still be sensitive in some environments, so access to them should be controlled and values possibly encrypted in transit.

The counters can reveal how much 6LoWPAN traffic a node handles. This might show whether a device is mostly idle and therefore perhaps "easier" to take away unnoticed. The reassembly counters could be used to direct denial-of-service attacks on the reassembly mechanism.

The RFC recommends the security features of SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Nobody can change the scoreboard, but peeking at it could tell a snoop when a gadget is quiet. So only the right people should be allowed to look.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The module uses an IANA-assigned object identifier recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: lowpanMIB is { mib-2 226 }. The object tree is shown as 1.3.6.1.2.1.226.
sections.eli5: The module was given its own official number so its scoreboard can always be found in the same place.
